title: Suicide or desperate cry for help? Inquest jury begins deliberations
subtitle: Cleve Geddes case exposed cracks in jail, mental health systems, advocate says
article: Did Cleve Geddes die by suicide or was his death an accidental hanging, a desperate effort by the 29-year-old paranoid schizophrenic to get staff at the Ottawa-Carleton Detention Centre to send him to hospital?
That question is one of many the five-person coroner's jury must answer as they began deliberations Friday on evidence given over eight days of testimony about Geddes' death in February 2017.

In addition to the mandatory "Five Ws" - who, where, when, why and by what means - jurors must also consider a list of dozens of recommendations given to them that could prevent similar deaths in the future.

"He should never have been in jail. That was the consensus we heard from everyone we heard from," said Irene Mathias, a volunteer with Mothers Offering Mutual Support, a group that advocates for incarcerated people and their families. "Cleve Geddes should not have been in jail. That's the tragedy."

Geddes was arrested in Killaloe, Ont., on Jan. 30, 2017 by OPP officers investigating a complaint that Geddes had threatened his father. Geddes was well known in town and had a long history of making threats, but no history of violence.

"How serious were the threats?" Mathias asked. "We heard so much evidence that leads me to believe that this was a man who was mentally ill screaming, shouting at the sky, at the world, in frustration."

A judge ordered Geddes to have a psychiatric assessment in hospital, but there were no beds available so he was sent to the OCDC instead. He spent more than a week there, often on suicide watch and in segregation, until guards found him unresponsive and hanging by his bedsheet while sitting in his cell. Did he intend to die?

"The forensic pathologist testified you have just 10 seconds to change your mind when hanging," Coroner's Counsel Tom Schneider said outside the inquest. Geddes had already tried a hunger strike as he pleaded with anyone he could find to be sent to a hospital.

Many of the suggested recommendations the jury must consider involve better training for police officers when dealing with the mentally ill and better communication. The guard on duty when Geddes hanged himself was never told he had just come off suicide watch, for example. Jurors also heard Geddes was unable to call his sister, Sigrid, because outgoing calls from the jail can't be made to a cellphone.
Jurors may also recommend the OCDC create a mental health unit, which was also a recommendation of the 2016 task force on the jail.

Paul Champ, lawyer for the Geddes family, wants jurors to push the province to proclaim Bill 6, which prohibits putting inmates with mental illness or on suicide watch into segregation. The bill has already received Royal Assent but has not been proclaimed by cabinet, he said.
"Technically, (Premier) Doug Ford could give it the force of law this afternoon," Champ said.
"The whole world knows that isolation and harsh conditions are damaging for people with mental illness," Mathias said.

"He endured it for days: cold conditions, uncomfortable clothing, complete lack of stimulation, no contact with people except through a meal hatch or passing by a little Plexiglas window and looking in on him like he was some kind of display animal in a zoo."
Mathias said the inquest exposed critical cracks in the system that swallowed Geddes up.

"As a society we failed this man from beginning to end," she said. "We failed him by not having adequate care in the community and by not having adequate mechanisms to get people like Cleve Geddes to hospital when he needed to be there."
Jurors are expected to return their verdict Monday when the inquest reconvenes under presiding coroner Dr. Michael B. Wilson.
